summary: A 1977 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols, such as protocol and port assignments. It replaced RFC 503 and RFC 604 and was replaced by RFC 750. It is historic.

eli5.summary: This was a big list of which number meant which thing in the network's rules, so everybody used them the same way.

subtitle: A registry of protocol numbers and reserved network addresses

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET and early internet grew, protocols and applications needed unique identifiers for links, sockets, networks, and message types to avoid conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 739 publishes a definitive list of all assigned numbers across multiple categories: ARPANET link assignments, socket assignments for standard functions and experimental uses, network numbers for interconnected networks, internet message versions and formats, and message types.
tldr.outcome: This registry provided a central source of truth, preventing conflicts and allowing independent implementations to interoperate. It was kept current periodically and replaced by RFC 750.

today: RFC 739 is Historic; it was replaced by RFC 750. The principle of maintaining a centralized registry of protocol numbers continues today through IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority).

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content: RFC 739 documents the currently assigned values from several series of numbers used in network protocol implementations. The RFC notes that it will be updated periodically, and current assignments can be obtained from Jon Postel at USC-ISI, who also handles new assignments. Developers building protocols or applications requiring link numbers, socket numbers, network numbers, or other standardized identifiers must contact Postel to receive assignments and avoid conflicts.
sections.eli5: The network is growing and needs to organize which numbers mean what. This list says who is in charge of giving out numbers and what each one is used for.

sections.title: Link, Socket and Network Numbers
sections.content: The RFC assigns links (which refer to an 8-bit field in the ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader, now part of a 12-bit message-id) in ranges for different uses: AHHP control messages, regular messages, reserved ranges, experimental protocols and specialized services like PARC protocols and TIP (Terminal IMP) reporting. Socket numbers are assigned for network-wide standard functions (0-63), host-specific functions (64-127), reserved ranges (128-223), and experimental uses (224-255). Network numbers identify different physical networks in the growing internet, including the ARPANET, various packet radio networks, CYCLADES, TELENET and others.
sections.eli5: Links, sockets and networks each get number ranges. Some numbers are for standard things like file transfer, others are for experiments, and some are reserved for later.

sections.title: Message Versions and Types
sections.content: The RFC specifies a 4-bit field identifying the version of the internet protocol (current version is 1, with 0 being older and 2-14 unassigned), and an 8-bit field identifying the format of the host-level protocol (raw internet, TCP-3, and DSP among the early formats). A separate 4-bit message type field distinguishes between different kinds of messages: escape, TCP-2, secure, gateway, measurement, DSP, UCL, and reserved types.
sections.eli5: Messages need to say what version they use and what kind they are, so computers know how to read them.
